precepts.text: Jacob refused to move his right hand from Ephraim's head, saying the younger brother shall be greater; he set Ephraim before Manasseh.
precepts.point: Jacob set that in place. When Joseph saw his father lay his right hand upon Ephraim's head it displeased him, and he tried to move it to Manasseh's head; but Jacob refused and said, his younger brother shall be greater than he; and he set Ephraim before Manasseh.

note.label: Genesis 41: Pharaoh's Dreams and Joseph's Rise Over Egypt

precepts.why:
Ephraim was the second born, but Jacob set him first. When Joseph saw his father lay his right hand upon Ephraim’s head, “it displeased him”, and he held up his father’s hand to move it to Manasseh’s head: “Not so, my father: for this is the firstborn; put thy right hand upon his head.” Jacob refused: “I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.” And “he set Ephraim before Manasseh.”

That is why Ephraim, the one named for God making Joseph fruitful in the land of his affliction, possessed the kingship, and not Manasseh the firstborn. The first king of the Northern Kingdom, Jeroboam, was of the tribe of Ephraim, and Ephraim is the head tribe of the Northern Kingdom. Jacob set that in place with his right hand.

precepts.text: Let my name be named on them, and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth.
precepts.point: And they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh: the blessing on Jacob's grandsons was to grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth. The Most High gets geographic with it: they went from the east to the west and multiplied in the midst of the hemisphere, in Central America.

note.label: Deuteronomy 33: The Blessing of Moses, Identifying the Tribes in the Last Days

precepts.why:
“and they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh.” The ten thousands and the thousands go back to the blessing Jacob put on his grandsons: “The Angel which redeemed me from all evil, bless the lads; and let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers Abraham and Isaac; and let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth.”

Jacob's name was named on the lads, which is why Ephraim and Manasseh stand as tribes of Israel, and they were to grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth. The Most High gets geographic with it: they went from the east to the west and multiplied in the midst of the hemisphere, in Central America. That is the ten thousands of Ephraim and the thousands of Manasseh.

precepts.text: Joseph brought his two sons Manasseh and Ephraim to his sick father, and Israel strengthened himself and sat upon the bed, glad to see his son.
precepts.point: Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48, where Israel blessed Joseph's sons and crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
Joshua tells the house of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, “Thou art a great people, and hast great power”, and that they shall drive out the Canaanites though they have iron chariots. Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48.

“And it came to pass after these things, that one told Joseph, Behold, thy father is sick: and he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.” Joseph brought his two sons to his sick father, “and Israel strengthened himself, and sat upon the bed”, glad to see his son. This is the moment the two brothers were blessed, and where Ephraim's greater place began.

precepts.text: Israel's eyes were dim for age; he kissed and embraced Joseph's sons, saying he had not thought to see Joseph's face, and lo, God had shewed him his seed also.
precepts.point: Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48, where Israel blessed Joseph's sons and crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
“And Israel beheld Joseph’s sons, and said, Who are these? And Joseph said unto his father, They are my sons, whom God hath given me in this place.” Israel says bring them to me and I will bless them. “Now the eyes of Israel were dim for age, so that he could not see.” He kissed them and embraced them, and said, “I had not thought to see thy face: and, lo, God hath shewed me also thy seed.”

Israel's eyes were dim for age; he could not see which son was which. Remember that, because what he does with his hands next is not by sight.

precepts.text: Joseph set Manasseh toward Israel's right hand for the greater blessing of the firstborn, but Israel stretched his right hand upon Ephraim the younger, guiding his hands wittingly.
precepts.point: Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48, where Israel blessed Joseph's sons and crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
“And Joseph took them both, Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel’s left hand, and Manasseh in his left hand toward Israel’s right hand, and brought them near unto him.” Joseph set Manasseh toward Israel's right hand for the greater blessing of the firstborn. “And Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it upon Ephraim’s head, who was the younger, and his left hand upon Manasseh’s head, guiding his hands wittingly; for Manasseh was the firstborn.”

Israel crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing. His eyes were dim, but this was no mistake. The right hand went on Ephraim the younger, and that is the root of why Ephraim drove out the Canaanites where Manasseh had issues.

precepts.text: It displeased Joseph and he held up his father's hand, but Israel refused, saying I know it, my son: Manasseh shall also be great, but his younger brother shall be greater, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.
precepts.point: Manasseh had issues driving the Canaanites out, but Ephraim did it. The difference between the two brothers goes back to Genesis 48, where Israel blessed Joseph's sons and crossed his hands, guiding them wittingly, meaning he knew exactly what he was doing.

note.label: Joshua 17: The Lot of Manasseh and the Blessing of Ephraim

precepts.why:
“And when Joseph saw that his father laid his right hand upon the head of Ephraim, it displeased him: and he held up his father’s hand, to remove it from Ephraim’s head unto Manasseh’s head.” Joseph said, “Not so, my father: for this is the firstborn”. “And his father refused, and said, I know it, my son, I know it: he also shall become a people, and he also shall be great: but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations.”

Manasseh shall also be great, but Ephraim shall be greater. That is why Joshua can say to the house of Joseph, “thou shalt drive out the Canaanites, though they have iron chariots, and though they be strong”, and it is Ephraim that did it. Ephraim being greater goes into Ephraim becoming the head of the ten tribes, the head of the kingdom of Samaria; and it was Ephraim that led the charge, with the help of Issachar and Manasseh, that brought the ten tribes from the eastern hemisphere to the western hemisphere.

The Zondervan compact Bible dictionary, a tool to add to your arsenal, says Ephraim and Manasseh seem to have been bitter rivals, Manasseh being the larger group, but Ephraim asserting the more vigorous leadership, though they seem to have held their land in common for a time. Vigorous means very passionate, sometimes rough; that is the spirit the children of Ephraim have.

precepts.text: Joseph's two sons are Manasseh and Ephraim, and Ephraim became the head over Samaria.
precepts.point: This is why the Samaritan woman said the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans; Samaria was Ephraim's territory, the head of Ephraim, on the parcel of ground Jacob gave to Joseph, whose sons were Manasseh and Ephraim. She was telling Christ she was of the tribe of Ephraim dwelling in Samaria, and Christ, whose first duty was to bring light to the northern kingdom, spoke to her openly.

note.label: Acts 10: Cornelius and the Northern Kingdom Grafted In

precepts.why:
“And it came to pass after these things, that one told Joseph, Behold, thy father is sick: and he took with him his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.”

Joseph's two sons are Manasseh and Ephraim, and Ephraim became the head over Samaria. So the parcel of ground Jacob gave to Joseph is Ephraim's land, and a woman of Samaria is of the northern kingdom.

Joseph set Ephraim toward Israel's left hand and Manasseh toward his right, so the firstborn would get the right hand blessing; and Israel crossed his hands wittingly, guiding them knowingly, laying his right hand on Ephraim the younger.

points: Joseph was displeased and tried to move his father's hand, and Israel refused: I know it, my son, I know it. Manasseh also shall become a people, and he also shall be great; but truly his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his seed shall become a multitude of nations. And he set Ephraim before Manasseh: Ephraim is the head tribe of the northern kingdom.

Reading shown on the multitude of nations: as of recent estimates, roughly two thirds of people of Puerto Rican origin live in the fifty states and the District of Columbia rather than on the island, about 6 million on the mainland and only about 3 million on the island. That is displacement, and it also shows Ephraim scattered as a multitude; you find Ephraimites even in Hawaii, sent there to work the sugarcane fields.
